sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Diagnostic Dilemma
sections.description: The clinical narrative begins with a young male patient referred following incidental detection of hyperglycemia and glycosuria during an annual health examination. Despite lacking acute symptoms at the moment of discovery, he soon reported classic triad symptoms of uncontrolled diabetes: polydipsia, polyuria, polyphagia, and unintended weight loss. His laboratory workup revealed significant metabolic derangement, with a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) of 10.2%, a fasting glucose of 12.4 mmol/L, and a 2-hour post-load glucose of 19.8 mmol/L during an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Crucially, the absence of diabetic ketoacidosis distinguished him from typical presentations of insulin-deficient Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) requiring immediate emergency intervention. sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of HNF1A-MODY and Renal Glucose Handling
sections.description: To fully appreciate the clinical presentation of this patient, one must first understand the dual-pathway pathophysiology inherent to Hepatocyte Nuclear Factor 1-alpha (HNF1A)-MODY. Unlike Type 1 diabetes, which is driven by autoimmune destruction, or typical Type 2 diabetes, which is characterized primarily by peripheral insulin resistance, HNF1A-MODY stems from a specific genetic defect affecting the development and functional capacity of the pancreas and kidneys simultaneously. The *HNF1A* gene encodes a transcription factor that is ubiquitously expressed but plays a pivotal regulatory role in three key organs: the liver, the kidney, and the pancreatic $\beta$-cells. sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning: From Biochemistry to Molecular Confirmation
sections.description: The diagnostic journey for this young male patient began with the recognition of a clinical paradox: he presented with significant hyperglycemia and classic catabolic symptoms like weight loss and polydipsia, yet lacked the hallmarks of typical Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) or overt Type 2 Diabetes (T2D). His body mass index was 24.6 kg/m², placing him in the normal range, and physical examination revealed no acanthosis nigricans, making severe insulin resistance unlikely. Crucially, the initial workup included a comprehensive autoantibody panel targeting glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies (GADA) and insulinoma antigen-2 autoantibodies (IA-2A). sections.section_title: Therapeutic Decision Making and Precision Medicine Implementation
sections.description: The management trajectory of this case underscores the pivotal role of genetic diagnosis in refining therapeutic strategies for monogenic diabetes. Upon initial presentation, the patient exhibited classic signs of severe hyperglycemia with an HbA1c of 10.2%, accompanied by weight loss and glycosuria. Lacking immediate genetic confirmation, the clinical team adopted an empiric approach typical for newly diagnosed diabetes presenting with significant catabolic features: initiating basal-bolus physiology coverage with insulin degludec alongside agents targeting insulin resistance and incretin pathways, specifically metformin and saxagliptin.
